planting.note: Broadcast or drill after all danger of frost has passed into warm, workable soil; Koto is a shorter, more lodging-resistant selection developed by Cornell University and Kade Research that reliably outyields older buckwheat lines in short-season plantings.

directions: Broadcast seed roughly half an inch deep into a warm, well-worked seedbed once the soil has warmed after the last frost, since Koto germinates within days and forms a dense canopy fast enough to smother emerging weeds. Bred as a shorter, sturdier, more stress-tolerant alternative to older buckwheat varieties, it holds up better to wind and rain without lodging while still flowering within about a month of sowing. Mow or till it under at first bloom to capture peak biomass before it sets seed, since it will readily volunteer if allowed to mature; its abundant, easily accessible flowers are also a favorite of honeybees and other pollinators during the brief but intense bloom window.
sources: SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Buckwheat

common_name: AU Sunrise Crimson Clover (Early-Blooming Reseeding Crimson Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring legume cover crop; AU Sunrise, released jointly by Auburn University and the USDA NRCS Jimmy Carter Plant Materials Center, blooms up to two weeks earlier than AU Robin and three weeks earlier than Dixie at lower latitudes.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a prepared seedbed in fall so plants can establish before the first hard freeze, then overwinter as a low rosette before resuming vigorous growth in late winter. AU Sunrise was specifically selected for very early flowering, which lets it complete seed set and reseed itself well ahead of the date a following summer crop needs the ground, an advantage over standard crimson clover strains that mature later in the Gulf South's mild winters. Its brilliant crimson flower spikes open earlier than almost any other winter annual legume, providing a critical early nectar source for emerging native bees while the plant fixes nitrogen and suppresses winter weeds. Because it reseeds so reliably, a single planting can sustain a self-renewing crimson clover stand across several seasons if allowed to shatter seed before termination.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Jimmy Carter Plant Materials Center

common_name: Pasja Hybrid Forage Brassica (Turnip-Rape Cover Crop Hybrid)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in late summer for a fast-growing fall cover crop, or sow in early spring; Pasja is a turnip × rape hybrid bred specifically for rapid leafy growth and quick regrowth after cutting or grazing.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since Pasja germinates quickly and reaches a leafy, grazable or mowable stage in as little as seven to eight weeks, faster than either straight turnips or straight forage rape. As a hybrid between forage turnip and forage rape, it combines the rapid regrowth of turnip with the leafiness of rape, tolerating repeated cutting or grazing better than most other cover crop brassicas while still building a modest taproot that helps break up compacted soil. Its abundant, tender foliage breaks down rapidly once winterkilled or incorporated, releasing nutrients quickly ahead of a following crop, and it can be interseeded with cereal rye or clover to extend fall groundcover.
sources: Cornell University Cover Crop Guide for NY Growers
King's AgriSeeds Forage Turnip and Rape Cover Crop Fact Sheet

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all danger of frost in fast-draining, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; desert milkweed is nearly leafless, photosynthesizing through its slender gray-green stems, and is exceptionally tolerant of heat and reflected sun once established.

directions: Sow or transplant into sharply-draining, sandy or rocky soil in full sun once temperatures are reliably warm, since seedlings are frost-tender until established; established plants tolerate extreme heat and long dry spells common in the Sonoran and Mojave deserts where the species is native. Its rush-like, nearly leafless stems bear clusters of small cream-to-yellow flowers over a long summer bloom period, making it a low-water, low-maintenance nectar source in xeriscape and desert pollinator gardens where showier milkweeds struggle. It is an important larval host plant for monarch and queen butterflies in the desert Southwest, and its architectural, upright form makes it useful as a background or specimen plant in native landscaping.

subcategory: southwestern native evergreen perennial pollinator plant

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, gravelly soil in full sun; pineleaf milkweed forms a shrubby, evergreen clump of fine, pine-needle-like foliage and blooms nearly continuously in warm climates.

directions: Plant in sharply-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun after the last frost; pineleaf milkweed is native to the Sonoran Desert borderlands of Arizona, Texas, and Mexico and forms a rounded, woody-based, shrubby perennial with fine, needle-like leaves that give it an almost conifer-like texture unlike any other milkweed. Small clusters of white flowers appear repeatedly through the warm months, drawing native bees and butterflies, and the plant serves as a larval host for monarch and queen caterpillars in low-desert gardens. Its low water needs and evergreen, well-behaved habit make it a popular structural choice in southwestern xeriscape and pollinator plantings.

subcategory: California native chaparral perennial pollinator wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; California milkweed benefits from natural winter chilling and rainfall to break seed dormancy, then goes summer-dormant after flowering in its native chaparral and foothill habitat.

directions: Sow seed in fall so winter rain and cold can naturally break dormancy, in lean, rocky or sandy soil with excellent drainage and full sun; this species is native to dry chaparral, foothill, and coastal sage scrub habitats of California and goes dormant in summer after its distinctive deep maroon-purple flowers fade. The thick, woolly gray-green leaves and unusually dark flower color set it apart from most other milkweed species, and it requires very little supplemental water once established, making it well suited to Mediterranean-climate native gardens. Like other milkweeds it serves as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies and provides nectar for a range of native bees during its spring bloom.
